News / TradingView / Key facts: SpaceX raises $86B in record IPO; Texas approves $24B project

Key facts: SpaceX raises $86B in record IPO; Texas approves $24B project 1 min read

SPCX SpaceX completed a record U.S. IPO in June at a $1.8 trillion valuation, or about 92 times trailing 12-month revenue. Shares remain above the IPO price but below their opening price. Reuters Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) raised about $85.7 billion to $86.2 billion in its June IPO, up from $75 billion after underwriters bought additional shares.

2 sources Texas approved SPCX’s $24 billion Rio Grande Valley data center and gas-power project. Its permit allows 35 turbines producing up to 750 megawatts, operating off-grid. Invezz Billionaire Len Blavatnik has built a stake in Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX) worth about $5 billion, Bloomberg reported. His firm, Access Industries, has invested in the company since 2020. Reuters SPCX denied imposing new Starlink restrictions after Ukraine said terminal limits hindered drone defenses. U.S. senators asked the company to preserve records on Ukraine’s access to the service. Benzinga SPCX plans its first orbital computing satellite launch in 2027, constellation expansion in 2028 and gigawatt-scale capacity by 2029. The firm expects existing business to fund much of the buildout. Benzinga SPCX completed the first tower catch of an intact Starship upper stage after reentry during Flight 15. Booster 22 was lost over the Gulf of Mexico; the recovery failure is under investigation. MarketBeat The FAA authorized SpaceX (SPCX) to launch Starship up to 25 times a year from Starbase, Texas. The company is also preparing to expand Starship operations in Florida. MarketBeat Musk said Anthropic will likely keep renting SpaceX computing capacity and may seek another 10 gigawatts, though AI restrictions could curb demand.

2 sources Elon Musk said Tesla and SpaceX (SPCX) may be better together, citing AI, robotics and chip advances, but said the companies could also pursue opportunities separately. item.content:encoded:
News / TradingView / Key facts: NVIDIA beats; shares fall on probe; China chip curbs

Key facts: NVIDIA beats; shares fall on probe; China chip curbs 1 min read

NVDA NVIDIA beat third-quarter revenue and earnings estimates, led by Data Center demand. Its fourth-quarter revenue forecast topped consensus, while the company raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook.

3 sources NVIDIA shares fell 2.2%, extending losses to five sessions, after a House committee sought a briefing on alleged export-control evasion involving customer Megaspeed. The allegations remain unproven.

3 sources The U.S. Commerce Department plans to restrict China’s access to NVIDIA’s advanced chips in overseas data centers and curb chip smuggling and Chinese firms’ use of Southeast Asian computing capacity.

3 sources NVIDIA (NVDA) shares fell as much as 14% Thursday after Huang’s departure was announced, hitting a nearly 16-month low before trimming losses to close down 4.3%. Reuters The SEC is investigating whether NVIDIA misled investors or inaccurately described its business in disclosures. The agency has not clarified the probe’s scope or focus.

2 sources Jefferies estimates new U.S. restrictions could cut NVIDIA’s data center revenue by $44 billion to $62 billion next year. Rules also target data centers remotely serving Chinese customers. Benzinga NVIDIA plans to file its 10-Q in the coming weeks and has posted interim financial details online. Michael Burry is watching its rising collection time and awaiting the filing.

2 sources NVDA traded nearly 37% below its October high, at about 10 times next-year earnings and below key moving averages. Its RSI was in the low 20s; NVIDIA cited shipment timing and extended payment terms.

2 sources NVIDIA halted licensed Hopper shipments to China; its outlook excludes future sales there. China generated $2.4 billion in third-quarter sales, while demand elsewhere is expected to offset the loss.

3 sources U.S. officials asked NVIDIA whether it knew its AI chips were allegedly transferred to China in breach of export rules. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent requested the company respond within ten days.
